prompt: Invent a short myth explaining why the sea is salty, in your own style.
task_completions:
Long ago, when the world was still cooling from the forge of creation, the ocean was not salt, but a vast, shimmering mirror of sweet, fresh water. In those days, the Moon was not a distant stone, but a silver-skinned giant who walked the shores, hopelessly in love with the Spirit of the Deep.

The Spirit of the Deep was a creature of current and coral, fluid and forever changing. She loved the Moon, but they were divided by a cruel law of the cosmos: the Moon belonged to the silence of the heights, and the Spirit belonged to the crushing weight of the abyss. They could only touch during the eclipses, brief moments where the sky kissed the tide.

For eons, the Moon spent his nights leaning over the edge of the world, whispering poetry to the waves. He brought the Spirit gifts from the stars—stardust, comet-tails, and frozen light—but these things dissolved in her embrace, leaving her longing for something more permanent, something that could bind them together.

One night, the Moon could bear the distance no longer. He descended from his throne, casting aside his celestial crown, and dove headlong into the ocean to be with his beloved. 

But the laws of the universe are stubborn. The moment the Moon’s silver skin touched the fresh water, the magic of the heavens clashed with the magic of the deep. The collision was not violent, but heartbreaking. As the Moon tried to merge his essence with the Spirit, his celestial form began to dissolve. He did not die, but he broke—shattering into a trillion tiny, crystalline tears of pure, white longing.

The Spirit of the Deep wept as she felt him dissolve into her, wrapping her currents around the remnants of his soul. She could not pull him back to the sky, so she absorbed him entirely, weaving his silver grief into every drop of her being.

The ocean turned from sweet to salt—the taste of a love so vast it could not be contained, and a sorrow that refuses to evaporate. To this day, the tides still rise and fall, the ocean reaching upward in a rhythmic, eternal attempt to touch the empty space where the Moon once stood.

Long ago, when the world was still cooling from the forge of creation, the Ocean was not a wild thing, but a vast, shimmering mirror of sweet, fresh water. In those days, the Ocean was the keeper of the world’s memories, holding every secret whispered into the wind and every dream dreamt by the first creatures.

Living beneath the sapphire waves was the Archivist, a colossal whale made of starlight and current. It was the Archivist’s duty to guard the "Great Crystal of Sorrow," a diamond the size of a mountain that absorbed every grief, every heartbreak, and every lonely tear shed by the inhabitants of the dry lands. The Crystal acted as a filter, keeping the world’s sadness locked away so that the land might remain hopeful and the air light.

For eons, the Archivist sang to the Crystal, lulling the sorrow into a deep, frozen sleep. But the Archivist grew lonely. It spent its immortality watching the love and laughter of the surface world, longing to feel the sting of a heartbreak or the ache of a longing—for to be immune to pain is also to be immune to the deepest kinds of love.

One evening, driven by a sudden, desperate curiosity, the Archivist pressed its massive heart against the Great Crystal and whispered, *"Let me feel."*

The Crystal, sensing a void to fill, did not merely share a spark; it shattered. 

In a single, thunderous instant, a billion years of accumulated grief, regret, and longing exploded into the sweet waters. The shockwave sent tsunamis crashing into the shores, and the pure water of the sea was instantly stained by the brine of a trillion tears.

The Archivist survived, but it was no longer made of starlight; it became a creature of flesh and bone, capable of feeling the crushing weight of the world's sadness. 

To this day, the sea remains salty because it carries the memory of everything the world has lost. And when the tide pulls back from the shore, it is the Ocean sighing, forever tasting the bittersweet salt of a heart that finally learned how to break.

In the First Age, the ocean was not salt, but a vast, shimmering mirror of sweet, fresh water. It was the domain of Olo, the Weaver of Tides, a giant spider made of sea-foam and moonlight who spent her eons knitting silver currents to keep the world’s temperatures in balance.

Olo was a creature of meticulous order, but she possessed one great weakness: she was a collector of sorrows.

Whenever a mortal on land wept—whether from a broken heart, a lost love, or a failed harvest—their tears did not simply sink into the earth. They drifted as invisible mists, drawn by the magnetic pull of Olo’s silver webs. Olo believed that sorrow was too heavy for a human soul to carry alone, so she caught every tear in her webs, pulling the grief out of the air and storing it in great, crystalline spheres at the bottom of the deep.

For millennia, Olo gathered the world's misery, keeping the land light and the people hopeful. But sorrow, when concentrated, becomes a heavy, corrosive thing. The crystalline spheres grew too large and too pressurized; they began to crack under the weight of a billion heartbreaks.

One Tuesday, in a sudden, violent chain reaction, every single sphere shattered at once.

The concentrated essence of every tear ever shed dissolved instantly into the fresh waters. The sweetness of the sea was vanished in a heartbeat, replaced by the sharp, stinging brine of a million years of human grief.

Olo wept for her failure, but her tears only added to the salinity. Now, the sea remains salt as a permanent archive of everything the world has lost—and it is why, when we swim in the ocean, the water tastes like the things we have forgotten how to mourn.
